title: Certainty and Stance in Writing
text:
Academic writers rarely state their claims with absolute confidence, preferring instead to signal how certain they are. Hedges such as 'may', 'appears to', and 'it is possible that' allow a writer to qualify a claim without abandoning it. Boosters, by contrast, express strong conviction and can make a text sound authoritative. Choosing between the two is a matter of stance, not simply of grammar.

Overuse of boosters can be risky, because readers may judge a writer who is always certain as careless or overconfident. A cautious formulation such as 'the data suggest' invites readers to evaluate the evidence themselves. Yet excessive hedging can also weaken an argument, leaving readers unsure what the writer actually believes. Effective writers therefore calibrate their certainty to the strength of the evidence.

questions.text: According to the passage, what do hedges allow a writer to do?
options: Express strong conviction without any evidence.
Qualify a claim without abandoning it.
Avoid making any claims at all.
Make the text sound more authoritative.

questions.text: According to the passage, what can excessive hedging do?
options: Make readers judge the writer as careless.
Weaken an argument by leaving readers unsure of the writer's belief.
Invite readers to evaluate the evidence themselves.

questions.text: What can be inferred about a writer who is always certain?
options: They are probably a more effective writer.
They may risk seeming overconfident to readers.
They rarely use any evidence in their work.
They avoid all boosters in their writing.

questions.text: Why does the writer conclude that effective writers calibrate their certainty?
options: Because readers expect every claim to be stated as a certainty.
Because hedging is always preferable to boosting.
Because the strength of their language should match the strength of the evidence.
Because the grammar of academic English requires it.

vocabulary.definition: a writer's attitude or position towards a claim or topic
to limit or add conditions to a statement
more certain of something than the evidence justifies
to adjust something so that it matches a required level

paragraph_translations: Escritores acadêmicos raramente apresentam suas afirmações com confiança absoluta, preferindo sinalizar o quanto estão seguros. Atenuadores como 'may', 'appears to' e 'it is possible that' permitem qualificar uma afirmação sem abandoná-la. Já os reforçadores expressam convicção forte e podem tornar o texto mais autoritário. Escolher entre os dois é uma questão de postura, e não apenas de gramática.

O uso excessivo de reforçadores pode ser arriscado, pois os leitores podem julgar um autor que está sempre certo como descuidado ou excessivamente confiante. Uma formulação cautelosa, como 'the data suggest', convida os leitores a avaliar as evidências por conta própria. No entanto, atenuar em excesso também pode enfraquecer um argumento, deixando os leitores inseguros sobre o que o autor realmente acredita. Autores eficazes, portanto, calibram sua certeza de acordo com a força das evidências.
